sources.headline: What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?
sources.text: The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections.As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US Congress helped end the Vietnam War. Can it stop the Iran war?list 2 of 3Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 with North Carolina seatlist 3 of 3Trump criticises Schumer amid push for new Democrat leadership in US Senateend of listAll the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats.Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office.How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? Find out in this quick explainer.What do the results say?The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years.The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran, aggressive immigration raids and corruption.Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.Which races remain?Four House seats have yet to be called: one in Minnesota, one in Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will be settled by a run-off on December 12.Those races could see the Democrats further expand their majority in the House. The final count is now a question of just how large the party’s majority will be.What will Democrats do with their majority?Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda.But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda.In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump.Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations.Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding.Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas.On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation.What role will Trump play?While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.Some lawmakers, however, have tried to persuade the president that he could benefit from working with Democrats after his party’s stark defeat in the midterms.Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, for example, has shared a series of tongue-in-cheek social media posts suggesting that a universal healthcare programme — a long-term progressive goal — could be named after the president in a bid to win his support.“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed said in a social media post showing a card for a hypothetical health insurance programme titled “Trumpcare”. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”Could Trump work with the Democrats?There is little evidence, however, to suggest that Trump is planning a political pivot after the midterms.Within a week of the vote, for instance, Trump named Stephen Miller — one of the architects of his hardline policies on immigration — as White House chief of staff.The staffing shake-up was seen as a doubling-down on right-wing policy priorities.While Trump has, at times, suggested that he could cooperate with Democratic lawmakers, he has also promised to use his veto power aggressively.He has also taken to social media to disparage Chuck Schumer, who is currently seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, a position he previously held from 2021 to 2025.“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”Trump’s White House has also threatened to take action if Democrats aggressively use their oversight powers in Congress.“Members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress” the constitutional limits of their power, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote in a letter on November 9, gesturing to the prospect of congressional investigations.

sources.headline: Democrats win House by largest margin in 50 years. And, COP31 ends with no deal
sources.text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories Vote counts are concluding for the 2026 midterm elections, revealing a better picture of just how much Democrats dominated. Fifty-six percent of voters chose the Democrats in House races compared to 42% for Republicans. The 14-point gap is the largest margin won by Democrats in 50 years. The party has officially won the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. Take a look at NPR's breakdown of the U.S. House races, by the numbers.
Julianna Conley/NPR
Artificial intelligence is causing significant swings in the stock market as investors speculate about the future of the technology boom. While AI stocks have driven markets to record highs and bolstered the economy, concerns are growing about a potential bubble. Investors anticipated that AI giant Anthropic's stock market debut last week would lift markets, but instead Wall Street experienced one of its worst weeks in recent times. 🎧 The National Association for Business Economics released a survey asking firms about their AI experiences. NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First that one in five reported measurable, widespread productivity gains, while about half said they saw some gains, but they weren't widespread. About 30% were either not using AI or felt it was too soon to assess its impact. Austan Goolsbee, head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, pointed out that the significant investment in AI is already affecting the economy, contributing to inflation by increasing demand for construction materials and electronic components. Although proponents believe AI could eventually help lower costs and limit inflation, Goolsbee tells Horsley that the Federal Reserve must address inflation challenges right now.
Poland has called an emergency NATO session for today after Russia fired three cruise missiles into its territory. The incident highlights the stakes for European countries in Russia's war on Ukraine, prompting nations along NATO's eastern border to seek enhanced air defense support. Poland plans to present proposals to increase surveillance capabilities and deploy more F-35s to intercept incoming missiles and drones. 🎧 Anti-missile systems and NATO flights were activated successfully, but Polish authorities say that poor weather prevented them from intercepting the incoming Russian missiles, according to reporter Teri Schultz. No injuries or damage were reported. More than a year ago, NATO established the Eastern Sentry to enhance air defense after a significant drone swarm from Russia entered Poland. Experts are now scrutinizing potential gaps in this defense. If this attack was deliberate by Moscow, Russia is risking severe consequences by endangering the lives of people on the ground in a NATO country, Schultz says. Delegates at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, couldn't agree on a plan over the weekend to address fossil fuels, the main cause of climate change. The event ran two days longer than expected, making it the longest in the history of these summits. Nearly 200 nations failed to finalize targets for electrification and financial aid for developing countries, or to address the impacts of climate change. The European Union rejected any conclusion that didn't advocate for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed this position. Fossil fuels contribute about 73% of global emissions.
🎧 Ultimately, the EU decided that no COP deal was better than a deal that didn't address fossil fuels, NPR's Rachel Waldholz says. She adds that money was another major issue. Developing nations sought increased support to tackle climate change, noting that they've contributed very little to climate change but often deal with the worst impacts. Wealthy nations agreed to provide funding under the Paris Climate Agreement. The U.S. was absent from the discussions due to the Trump administration's withdrawal from international climate negotiations. Many smaller and developing nations are strong defenders of these talks, viewing them as a vital platform to ensure their voices are heard alongside larger countries, Waldholz says. Books We Love
NPR
NPR's annual reading guide, Books We Love, is back with more than 380 new recommendations from staff and trusted critics. This year's picks span a range of genres, including fiction, cookbooks, children's reads, poetry and science fiction. Don't worry if it looks overwhelming; the interactive filters will help you narrow down your list and find your next great read. And why stop at this year's reads? The Books We Love archive has 14 years of recommendations, so you can discover more than 4,700 amazing books, all in one place. This year's edition of Books We Love is dedicated to Rose Friedman, who edited a dozen editions and worked at NPR for 15 years before her death this year at age 38. Friedman was one of the original founders of Books We Love, formerly known as The Book Concierge. In her honor, start exploring and find something wonderful to read today. Behind the story by Maria Godoy, senior science and health editor and correspondent
Clinical services supervisor Dale Weiser poses for a portrait at the Chester County Health Department in West Chester, Pa., on Oct. 28, 2026.
Daniel Vasta for NPR

Daniel Vasta for NPR
People had warned me it might be tough to get Amish people to talk to me as a journalist — and probably impossible to get their permission to record their voice. Not a great omen for compelling radio storytelling.
Yet as I headed off to Lancaster County, Pa., last month to report on the biggest and deadliest measles outbreak in the U.S. in decades, I knew I wanted to hear directly from the community hit hardest. So I turned to some good old shoe-leather reporting. My producer and I mapped out Amish-owned businesses in and around Lancaster County and spent a day driving around from shop to shop. At every stop, we introduced ourselves and explained the focus of our story. We asked Amish people (easily identifiable by their traditional dress) about their views on the measles outbreak and vaccination. While some declined to talk, others opened up about how measles had affected their families and communities, and why they had or hadn't decided to get vaccinated. To my surprise, one woman even let me record her voice. Outside a farm supply store in a rural town, I met an Amish woman who was visibly pregnant. Measles can have devastating consequences during pregnancy. She told me her husband and two children had gotten vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She declined to give me her name at first, then got in a car driven by her hired non-Amish driver. As they exited the parking lot, the driver stopped to ask us what media outlet we were with. "Oh, NPR!" the driver said when we replied. Then she turned to her Amish passenger and told her, "Don't worry, you can trust them." Part of gaining trust is about showing up, showing respect and really listening. Word gets around that you're trustworthy. Public health officials in Pennsylvania have also been using a similar approach to win the trust of Amish people as they seek to boost vaccination rates in the current outbreak. You can read more about it here.

Bayer could pay up to $7.25 billion to settle lawsuits alleging that its weed-killer Roundup caused cancer. A Missouri judge gave final approval to the nationwide settlement.South Africa's grassroots program Read Alex is tackling a children's literacy crisis and inspiring kids to write. The initiative culminated in a book launch for an anthology titled From Gomora to the World, showcasing stories written by children.Orchestra Noir transforms 2000s hip-hop and R&B classics into high-energy, choreographed symphonic shows. Beyond delivering performances, the all-Black ensemble creates a cultural bridge through their post-show ritual, when musicians meet with their multigenerational audiences. sources.headline: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
sources.text: Figure caption, Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'ByMadeline HalpertUpdated 23 November 2026The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called. Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats. View the 2026 midterm election resultsSunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%."I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable. Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of RepresentativesHubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx two years ago by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa. Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters. Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website. The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes. Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law. However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation. Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

Democrat Hubbard wins North Carolina recount, clinching historic House majority

Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the US House of Representatives from North Carolina on Sunday after defeating veteran Republican Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerful House Rules Committee. His victory gave Democrats their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in the 2026 US midterms.

Issued on: 22/11/2026 - 21:16
Modified: 23/11/2026 - 08:33

  4 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
Chuck Hubbard speaks to the press in Washington DC on November 8, 2026. © Nathan Howard, AP

House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018. 

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats’ majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300. 

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

“There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome".

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Read morePeltola defeats Sullivan in Alaska Senate race, expanding Democratic majority

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire. 

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol. 

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change”.

Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

“Everything should be tied back to the people – and how it’s affecting the people,” he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: “How does that affect people’s pocketbooks?”

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations – a standard oversight function of Congress – may amount to “blatant criminality”.

After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority – meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda – the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver. 

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith – people come to the caucus with different ideas – it's OK,” said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus. 

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994. 

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power. 

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.

The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)

sources.headline: Midterms: US Democrats secure biggest House majority in decades
sources.text:
The Democrats have won at least 258 seats in the 435-member House, gaining 44 from Republicans in its strongest general election performance since 1992.
The latest victory came in North Carolina, where Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated veteran Republican congresswoman Virginia Foxx. Four House races have yet to be decided, with contests in Minnesota and Tennessee still awaiting a result and two Louisiana races heading to runoffs in December.
The result surpasses the Democrats' gains in the 2018 midterm elections, when they picked up 40 seats during Trump's first presidency. Republicans are now set to hold no more than 177 seats, leaving them with one of their smallest House delegations in decades.
The Democratic wave extended across traditional Republican strongholds, the Midwest and the East Coast, reflecting widespread voter frustration over the cost of living, the war in Iran and allegations of corruption surrounding the Trump administration.
Democrats will also control the Senate, where they have secured 56 seats, giving the party its strongest position in Congress in more than a decade.
An ambitious agenda — and high expectations
With control of both chambers from January, Democrats are preparing an ambitious first 100 days focused on household finances, healthcare and government accountability.
Their priorities include reversing Republican cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired under Republican control. The party also intends to use congressional investigative powers to scrutinise Trump's administration, including the financial interests of the president and his family.
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, is expected to become the first Black Speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on 3 January 2027.
Unlike outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, who struggled to manage a razor-thin majority, Jeffries would have considerable room to accommodate disagreements between progressive and moderate Democrats.
Nevertheless, the scale of the victory has raised expectations that the party will produce tangible results.
“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” Democratic congressman Jason Crow of Colorado told the Associated Press, pointing to Americans struggling with healthcare costs, economic insecurity and immigration enforcement.
Progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez described the election result as “a mandate for change”, while centrist Democrat Tom Suozzi argued that the party should devote most of its attention to affordability rather than investigations.
Confrontation with the White House
The Democratic takeover threatens to significantly constrain Trump during the final two years of his presidency.
Congressional committees are expected to launch investigations into the administration, potentially issuing subpoenas and demanding testimony from senior officials. Jeffries has also declined to rule out a third impeachment attempt against Trump.
The White House has responded aggressively, suggesting that some proposed investigations could amount to criminal misconduct — a claim that has intensified tensions over Congress's constitutional oversight responsibilities.
Republicans, meanwhile, face a difficult period of rebuilding. Jim Jordan of Ohio, chosen to lead the party's diminished House minority, has pledged to fight for American families and regain political ground ahead of the 2028 elections.
For Democrats, however, the immediate challenge is turning an overwhelming electoral victory into effective government. Their substantial congressional majorities offer an unusual opportunity to advance legislation, but Trump's continued control of the White House means major bills could still face a presidential veto.
Fact is: The midterm elections have fundamentally shifted the balance of power in Washington.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They are far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Congressman Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.

The Republicans’ high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.
